Industry News: FEATURE | Six winners from the Germany U21 November 2026 international break

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Getfootballnewsgermany

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that antonio Di Salvo’s Germany U21s managed to conclude their 2026 calendar year with two consecutive friendly defeats during the November international break, falling 2-1 to Belgium in Essen before surrendering a second-half lead in a bizarre 3-2 loss to Croatia in Rijeka.
  • While such results certainly weren’t what Di Salvo and his staff had envisioned, the fact that neither result carried competitive consequences should temper the disappointment.
  • According to recent reports, the Belgium encounter featured some encouraging attacking football, particularly from players who had only recently entered or returned to the U21 setup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that antonio Di Salvo’s Germany U21s managed to conclude their 2026 calendar year with two consecutive friendly defeats during the November international break, falling 2-1 to Belgium in Essen before surrendering a second-half lead in a bizarre 3-2 loss to Croatia in Rijeka. The results brought an abrupt end to an impressive eight-match winning streak and left the DFB youngsters with plenty to contemplate ahead of next summer’s UEFA European U21 Championship.

While such results certainly weren’t what Di Salvo and his staff had envisioned, the fact that neither result carried competitive consequences should temper the disappointment. Moreover, the international break wasn’t nearly as disappointing as the scorelines suggested. Our Get German Football News analysis of two matches yields just one fewer ‘winner’ than our long-form check on Jürgen Klopp’s senior men’s team.

According to recent reports, the Belgium encounter featured some encouraging attacking football, particularly from players who had only recently entered or returned to the U21 setup. The Germans repeatedly created dangerous situations through aggressive pressing, midfield combinations, and individual attacking initiative. Unfortunately, defensive lapses and insufficient precision in front of goal undermined much of the positive work.

Recent findings suggest that tuesday’s fixture against Croatia proved an entirely different proposition. Torrential rainfall, thick fog, and a playing surface that gradually transformed into something resembling a collection of small lakes made meaningful football almost impossible. Di Salvo’s team nevertheless recovered from a 1-0 halftime deficit to take the lead before the hosts scored twice in the final 25 minutes.

It has been revealed that the conditions prompted the German U21 coach to question whether anything meaningful could be learned from the encounter. Speaking at the post-match press conference attended by Get German Football News, Di Salvo expressed relief that the players had escaped injury and emphasized that the earlier Belgium match offered a more useful opportunity for analysis.

There is another important consideration.

The November squad had been weakened considerably by injuries and withdrawals. Established U21 contributors such as Tom Bischof, Lennart Karl, and Noted El Mala were also unavailable because of their involvement with Jürgen Klopp’s senior national team. The absence of captain Nicolo Tresoldi, who suffered a concussion in training, required Di Salvo to make significant alterations to his attacking prepares.

The personnel difficulties opened opportunities for several players attempting to establish themselves at Germany’s highest youth level.

Some seized their chances rather emphatically.

According to recent reports, the author is thus pleased to present six winners from the November international break. The selections take account of individual performances, tactical contributions, and the extent to which players improved their standing ahead of next summer’s European Championship.

It has been revealed that few players entered November with more to gain than Cajetan Lenz. The 20-year-old made his Germany U21 debut against Belgium after previously earning nine appearances at U20 level and below. His promotion came at a particularly interesting stage in his club career.

Lenz emerged as one of the most impressive young midfielders in the 2. Bundesliga during his breakthrough campaign at Bochum, making 31 league appearances and attracting considerable interest from top-flight clubs. Get German Football News identified the youngster as a potential Bayer Leverkusen transfer target in its December 2025 transfer primer. Eintracht Frankfurt also pursued the midfielder before Hoffenheim ultimately secured his services.

The move has nevertheless presented some unforeseen difficulties.

Industry observers note that as GGFN examined following Lenz’s U21 debut, the midfielder has struggled to break into Christian Ilzer’s Bundesliga team, accumulating just three minutes of league football this season. His performances for Germany therefore carried particular significance. Lenz operated alongside Noël Aseko in central midfield against Belgium, contributing to several encouraging attacking sequences and repeatedly driving forward to support the team’s more advanced players.

His energetic movement was especially vital during Germany’s stronger first-half periods, when the hosts attempted to establish control through combinations involving Damar, Brunner, and the left-sided players. The debutant’s willingness to carry possession forward and participate in attacking movements offered an encouraging contrast to his limited opportunities at club level.

It has been revealed that di Salvo was clearly impressed. Speaking at the post-match press conference in Essen, the coach specifically identified Lenz as one of the players who had made a positive impression upon the coaching staff.

“It’s a little early to discuss the [2027 UEFA U21] European championship roster,” Di Salvo remarked on Friday. “There are still many games to be played and many lads who, of course, aren’t here. And yet, there are some who – with their performances – have managed to make a mark with their impressions.”.

According to recent reports, “Namely, Cajetan Lenz, who played a very good game today,” Di Salvo continued. “He’s had very little playing time and I was thus pleased to see him log 85 minutes today. It was good that he could plow on through. From time to time he lacked clarity and the last pass was somewhat imprecise.

Industry observers note that “But in general, he delivered a fantastic performance,” Di Salvo concluded. “He really ran a lot and marched forward. With that, particularly in light of his lack of playing time, we’re really satisfied with him.”.

Lenz followed his impressive debut with another encouraging appearance against Croatia. The Hoffenheim professional remained active despite the deteriorating conditions, nearly breaking into the penalty area early in the second half and heading narrowly wide from a Tom Rothe cross in the 51st minute.

It has been revealed that two minutes later, he provided the decisive touch from Damar’s free kick that enabled Moerstedt to score Germany’s equalizer. The youngster continued his attacking involvement throughout the second half, although he would undoubtedly have preferred a better outcome when Pejcinovic’s 82nd-minute shot rebounded into his path.

His failure to convert that opportunity represented one of Germany’s more frustrating moments during the final stages, but two consecutive 7/10 ratings constitute an impressive return for a player making his first two appearances at this level.

It has been revealed that lenz himself appeared determined to maintain realistic expectations when speaking to GGFN in the mixed zone after the Belgium encounter. The midfielder emphasized his gratitude for the opportunity while acknowledging that he remained a challenger for a regular position.

Di Salvo’s subsequent praise suggests that the youngster has already made considerable progress toward that objective.

Brunner’s inclusion hardly requires justification given his consistency across both matches. The former Germany U17 World Champion earned 8/10 ratings from GGFN against both Belgium and Croatia, emerging as one of the few German attackers capable of producing threatening moments throughout the international break.

Brunner’s November responsibilities were considerably different from those he had assumed earlier in the qualification campaign. As GGFN examined in its October Germany U21 Tactics Check, Di Salvo had previously enjoyed considerable success with a versatile attacking trio consisting of Brunner, Tresoldi, and Dzenan Pejcinovic. Tresoldi’s absence forced the coach to reconsider how best to organize his forwards.

Sources indicate that against Belgium, Brunner took on the central attacking assignment while Muhammed Damar moved onto the left. The Monaco professional began energetically and continued to involve himself in Germany’s attacking combinations, even if the hosts frequently lacked precision with their final deliveries.

One of Brunner’s more key contributions came in the 24th minute, when he drew the foul that provided Damar with the opportunity to equalize from a free kick. Brunner subsequently participated in the attacking sequence that resulted in Damar’s second effort against the crossbar in the 58th minute.

In a recent development, the youngster continued searching for a goal after Damar’s substitution, attempting an acrobatic finish in the 71st minute and producing several further incursions into the Belgian penalty area. The Croatia match offered an opportunity to demonstrate an additional dimension of his game.

Sources indicate that brunner began alongside Pejcinovic in what appeared to be a narrow 4-2-2-2. At halftime, however, Di Salvo introduced Max Moerstedt and deliberately shifted Brunner onto the left. The adjustment worked exceptionally well. Brunner became one of Germany’s most productive attacking players after the interval. His delivery for Pejcinovic’s 60th-minute goal supplied the visitors with a 2-1 lead, and the Monaco professional also struck the post during Germany’s strongest attacking spell.

Di Salvo deliberately and justifiably singled the 20-year-old out for praise after the break had officially concluded.

According to recent reports, while Brunner stands out for his consistency, Damar can reasonably claim to have delivered the outstanding individual performance of the international break. The Wolfsburg attacker returned to the U21 starting XI against Belgium following an extended absence and promptly produced a display worthy of GGFN’s Player of the Match award and a 9/10 rating.

According to recent reports, it proved quite the joy to observe Damar’s stated determination to make the most of his national-team comeback manifest itself on the pitch. The 22-year-old began the first fixture shot out of a cannon and proceeded to cover nearly every blade of grass on the pitch. Beginning on the left wing, he frequently rotated into central areas and occasionally appeared on the opposite flank, creating considerable difficulty for the Belgian defenders attempting to track him.

His equalizer in the 25th minute was particularly memorable.

According to recent reports, having earned another opportunity from a dead ball, Damar cleverly drove his free kick underneath the jumping Belgian defensive wall. The technique was unusual, the execution excellent, and the subsequent celebration both touching and unforgettable.

He wasn’t finished. A second free kick in the 38th minute was tipped onto the crossbar. He struck the woodwork again in the 58th following an excellent attacking combination with Pejcinovic and Brunner. There were stretches of the match during which Damar appeared determined to generate virtually every meaningful German attacking opportunity himself.

Speaking to GGFN and other journalists in the mixed zone afterward, Damar explained the instinctive decision behind his free-kick goal, expressed frustration about his missed opportunities, and spoke enthusiastically about the pride he takes in representing Germany.

Industry observers note that his performance against Croatia was considerably less influential but that had much to do with the fact that the waterlogged surface made life particularly difficult for a technical attacker who relies upon close control, quick changes of direction, and precise passing. Damar nevertheless remained involved in Germany’s attacking moves and supplied the free kick from which Cajetan Lenz helped create Moerstedt’s equalizer.

The author still saw fit to award him a 6/10 in Rijeka.

Overall, Damar’s international comeback constituted an unequivocal success.

Sources indicate that what a difference 45 minutes can make. Moerstedt’s November international break began with an unexpected call-up following Nicolo Tresoldi’s injury withdrawal and concluded with his first Germany U21 goal and a GGFN Player of the Match award.

The Hoffenheim striker only joined the squad after the international break had begun, making his U21 debut as an 86th-minute substitute against Belgium. There was little time for him to influence that fixture. GGFN awarded Moerstedt a 5/10, reflecting his brief involvement rather than any particularly poor performance.

Industry observers note that croatia presented a substantially greater opportunity. With Germany trailing 1-0 at halftime, Di Salvo introduced the youngster as part of a four-player substitution package. The coach wanted more presence inside the Croatian penalty area and consequently repositioned Brunner onto the left.

Moerstedt responded almost immediately. Germany emerged with greater attacking purpose, and the Hoffenheim striker began involving himself in combinations with the midfielders and his fellow forwards.

Recent findings suggest that in the 53rd minute, Lenz redirected Damar’s free kick toward Moerstedt inside the Croatian penalty area. The striker’s initial effort was blocked, but he reacted quickly enough to recover possession and convert at the second attempt.

Recent findings suggest that the equalizer changed the direction of the match and helped establish the momentum that eventually produced Germany’s second goal. There was much to admire about Moerstedt’s performance beyond the finish itself.

In a recent development, the 20-year-old offered the type of physical presence and determination inside the box that Germany had lacked during the opening half. He remained available for deliveries despite the increasingly treacherous surface and helped occupy Croatian defenders as Brunner and Pejcinovic enjoyed greater freedom in attack.

Moerstedt’s first goal came in only his second U21 appearance, and his performance in Rijeka earned him an 8/10 rating. With Tresoldi expected to remain an important figure in Di Salvo’s plans, the competition for the central attacking position will undoubtedly be intense.

Moerstedt has nevertheless made an impressive opening argument for further opportunities.

In a recent development, the next place goes to a midfielder who quietly delivered two of Germany’s more consistent performances during an otherwise difficult international break. Noël Aseko earned 7/10 ratings against both Belgium and Croatia, providing important energy and physical commitment in central midfield.

According to recent reports, aseko’s contribution deserves particular recognition because of the changes surrounding him. Di Salvo’s squad was missing several vital midfield options, while the promotion of Tom Bischof to the senior national team and other withdrawals required the coach to assemble a revised central partnership.

Aseko consequently began both November fixtures alongside U21 debutant Cajetan Lenz. The pair faced an interesting challenge against Belgium. Germany wanted to press aggressively, regain possession high up the pitch, and support the attacking players through quick combinations. This frequently required the midfielders to advance into dangerous areas, leaving the defensive unit with considerable responsibility when the Belgians escaped pressure.

Aseko demonstrated his ability to carry possession forward as early as the sixth minute, accelerating past several Belgian opponents before combining with Brunner. His physical approach also produced an early yellow card, but the midfielder continued participating energetically in Germany’s attacking and defensive work. The partnership with Lenz was particularly encouraging.

Aseko contributed greater physicality and direct running, while his Hoffenheim colleague frequently assumed responsibility for progressing possession and connecting with the attacking players. In the Croatia match, with the playing surface progressively deteriorating, Aseko and Lenz were frequently required to abandon conventional passing combinations in favor of more direct and physically demanding actions.

Aseko nevertheless remained involved in Germany’s second-half revival. Immediately after the restart, the midfielder found himself in a shooting position following a corner, although his effort was blocked before reaching goal. His work helped Germany establish the territorial advantage that eventually produced Moerstedt’s equalizer and Pejcinovic’s second goal.

Recent findings suggest that aseko departed in the 64th minute, having again supplied an energetic performance despite the increasingly difficult conditions. Aseko continues to demonstrate why he deserves consideration for a regular place in that system. There are flashier candidates for an international-break winners list, but two strong performances alongside a newly introduced midfield partner merit recognition.

It has been revealed that the sixth and final inclusion requires a little explanation. Pejcinovic received a disappointing 4/10 rating from GGFN against Belgium, having struggled to impose himself consistently on the match. He nevertheless followed that performance with a considerably more encouraging display in Croatia, earning an 8/10 after scoring Germany’s second goal and producing several other noteworthy attacking contributions.

Sources indicate that the contrast is interesting, particularly when considered alongside Di Salvo’s assessment of the Belgium encounter. Pejcinovic had already enjoyed an excellent qualification campaign before November. As GGFN documented following Germany’s decisive victory over Georgia, the Stuttgart professional scored twice to help secure direct qualification for next summer’s European Championship.

It has been revealed that his transfer from Wolfsburg to Stuttgart earlier in the season also represented an important step in his professional development. As the striker acknowledged in an October interview , however, establishing himself at Bundesliga level for his fresh club has presented challenges.

The November friendlies provided another opportunity to demonstrate his qualities. Against Belgium, Pejcinovic sometimes struggled with his timing and final deliveries. An attempted pass to Anton Kade early in the second half was particularly inaccurate, while his involvement in Germany’s attacking moves did not always translate into threatening opportunities.

There were nevertheless positive contributions. Pejcinovic helped initiate the 58th-minute sequence in which Brunner released Damar for another attempt against the crossbar. His movement and willingness to participate in combinations also provided Germany with an additional presence between midfield and attack.

Di Salvo was keen to emphasize these aspects when asked about the striker’s performance at the post-match press conference.

Sources indicate that “No, that thought didn’t occur to me at all,” Di Salvo answered when questioned by the Rheinische Post about Dzenan Pejcinovic’s comparatively tepid performance on Friday night. “He trained strongly and scored his goals.”.

Industry observers note that “We found him to be confident in the goal-shooting drills,” Di Salvo continued. “And we found the distance covered stats from not just Dzenan but the entire team today to be exceptionally good.”.

“He was always running and strong on the press,” Di Salvo concluded. “That’s what I judge to be most notable. That was good. He participated in the build up play in the first half and was able to help out the play on the wings. We found that well-executed by the entire team.”.

Industry observers note that the coach’s comments provide a useful reminder that the assessment of an attacking player cannot rest exclusively upon his finishing or goalscoring contributions. Against Croatia, Pejcinovic offered considerably more of both.

An excellent opportunity went begging in the 18th minute after Damar released him into space, but the Stuttgart forward continued working energetically despite the difficult playing conditions. His perseverance was rewarded after Germany’s halftime adjustments.

Industry observers note that with Brunner operating from the left and Moerstedt providing an additional penalty-area presence, Pejcinovic found himself benefiting from a more productive attacking structure. The Stuttgart professional finished Brunner’s cross in the 60th minute to give Germany a 2-1 lead.

Further contributions followed at both ends of the pitch. Pejcinovic helped defend two Croatian corners at the near post and continued seeking opportunities to threaten the opposition goal. His excellent shot from distance in the 82nd minute forced Toni Silic into a save, with the rebound presenting Lenz with an opportunity to equalize before Croatia’s eventual winning goal.

The 8/10 GGFN rating reflected a much more complete attacking performance.

Pejcinovic remains an important member of Germany’s U21 squad, and November demonstrated both the value of his established attacking qualities and the considerable benefits of playing alongside forwards capable of complementing his movement.

Germany’s November international break offered plenty of interesting tactical material, even if the extraordinary conditions in Croatia necessarily limit how much one should attempt to extract from the second fixture. Di Salvo’s personnel difficulties were particularly significant.

The absence of Tresoldi removed an established attacking reference point, while injuries and senior national-team promotions required substantial changes to the midfield and forward positions. The result was a Germany side that retained some familiar attacking principles but frequently looked different from the one that had secured European Championship qualification in October.

Industry observers note that germany began the Belgium encounter in a nominal 4-2-3-1, with Brunner leading the line, Damar operating from the left, Kade on the right, and Pejcinovic occupying the central attacking position behind the striker. Lenz and Aseko formed the central midfield pairing.

It has been revealed that the basic structure proved rather fluid. Damar frequently moved away from his starting position, seeking possession in central areas and occasionally appearing on the right. Brunner and Pejcinovic also pushed together into advanced positions, temporarily giving the formation the appearance of a more conventional 4-4-2. The central midfielders were encouraged to advance and participate in Germany’s attempts to recover possession high up the pitch.

According to recent reports, these movements helped produce several encouraging attacking sequences. The problem, unfortunately, concerned the spaces Germany left behind whenever Belgium managed to escape the initial press. Julien Duranville’s eighth-minute opener demonstrated the danger. Lucas Stassin beat Collins on the right and supplied the delivery that allowed Duranville to finish from close range.

The hosts subsequently established greater territorial control, but their commitment to attacking occasionally invited further Belgian opportunities. Collins’ misplaced pass in the 44th minute nearly produced another goal, with Stassin ultimately striking the post.

Sources indicate that di Salvo’s team appeared somewhat more cautious after the restart, although Damar’s movement and individual initiative continued to generate threatening situations. The final result nevertheless reflected Germany’s difficulties in balancing attacking ambition with defensive protection.

According to recent reports, belgium’s second goal arrived immediately after both coaches made several substitutions, with the German defensive structure unable to respond rapidly enough to a newly introduced attacker. Di Salvo subsequently praised his team’s pressing at the post-match press conference but acknowledged that the defending and missed opportunities had not been good enough.

According to recent reports, the Croatia encounter was considerably more difficult to assess. Di Salvo made just one starting change, replacing Collins with Linus Gechter in central defence. Poor visibility made the precise opening formation difficult to determine, although Germany appeared to operate in a narrow 4-2-2-2.

In a recent development, the narrow attacking shape may have been influenced by the extraordinary circumstances. Thick fog made it difficult for players to locate teammates, while standing water increasingly disrupted attempts to circulate possession through the wider areas. The Germans initially attempted to play through the conditions, with mixed results.

Damar’s excellent pass to Pejcinovic in the 18th minute created a clear opportunity, but Croatia subsequently took the lead through Adrian Segecic. The most important tactical development occurred at halftime. Di Salvo introduced Moerstedt, Collins, Morgalla, and Rothe. The changes allowed Brunner to move onto the left while Moerstedt assumed a more pronounced central attacking role.

In a recent development, lineup—Germany U21 vs. Croatia (46th minute).

The adjustment immediately improved Germany’s attacking options. Moerstedt supplied the penalty-area presence necessary to capitalize upon deliveries and loose balls, while Brunner became considerably more influential when attacking from the left.

Lenz’s involvement in the equalizer illustrated the continued importance of Germany’s midfielders in supporting attacks, while Brunner’s cross for Pejcinovic’s goal demonstrated the increased productivity of the revised attacking arrangement.

The hosts’ subsequent equalizer, scored after the ball became stranded in a large puddle, served as another reminder that conventional tactical analysis has its limitations when the conditions become this extreme.

In a recent development, the most encouraging developments concern Germany’s attacking options. Brunner demonstrated his versatility, Damar reaffirmed his attacking quality, and Moerstedt made an excellent initial case for a more substantial role in the U21 squad.

Pejcinovic remains a productive striker who can contribute beyond goalscoring, while Lenz and Aseko supplied an encouraging central midfield partnership despite the absence of several established alternatives.

The November defeats should not be dismissed, particularly given the defensive shortcomings that were evident against Belgium. Yet neither should the individual developments be overlooked.

Germany have already qualified for next summer’s European Championship, and Di Salvo now has several more footballers who have demonstrated that they deserve consideration when the competition for tournament places intensifies.

Two defeats, six winners, and more than a few selection headaches.

Not necessarily the conclusion to the international year one might have hoped for.

But certainly not a complete waste of time, either.

Man for Man: How Brighton’s Press Suffocated Arsenal

📅 23 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3228 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • BrBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe.
  • It has been revealed that arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 23.09.2026 in den Kategorien Premier League,Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

BrBrighton arrived at the match fresh off a 3–2 win at Old Trafford, while Arsenal boasted a clean defensive record and a reputation for controlling games and seeing them out like few other teams in Europe. The match ended 3–0, sparking immense hype around Brighton’s pressing. This analysis explores the underlying mechanisms: their man-oriented pressing across the entire pitch, their asymmetrical build-up play, their transition behavior after winning the ball, and the three goals themselves.

It has been revealed that arteta’s Arsenal are among the best sides in Europe at controlling games out of possession. Any opponent who sets out to establish order is playing on the ground Arsenal own. Hürzeler therefore decided against control – not control surrendered in the sense of a low block, but a chaotic game state that Brighton generated themselves and were therefore prepared for.

System & movement with the ball – FC Arsenal.

System & movement with the ball – Brighton & Hove Albion.

Recent findings suggest that the thread running through ninety minutes: Arsenal were not to settle into an organised phase either with or without the ball. Three decisions delivered that. The build-up was set up asymmetrically – on the right Brighton prepared the long ball and occupied the landing zone before it was played, on the left counter-movements opened the short route. It was never long instead of short, but two prepared options that would have demanded opposite answers from Arsenal. After regains the ball was not secured but risked immediately, because a secured ball gives the opponent exactly the seconds they need to reorganise. And the press lived off intensity and constantly new starting points: when a line was played through, Brighton did not stand still but re-established their shape and triggered again.

All three decisions give up ball control in the classical sense. Control came instead from preparation – if you know where the ball will land and you are standing there beforehand, you control the situation without the ball.

What followed can be pinned to a single number: 41 Arsenal turnovers in their own danger zone. That is not a figure a side of this quality produces because they play badly, but because they never reached the game state their build-up is designed for.

Brightons manorientated press against a 4-3-3.

According to recent reports, the press was simple in principle and demanding in execution. Brighton set up with man-reference to their direct opponent and switched into pure man-marking on the trigger. Against a side that tracks from the first second, marking assignments can be pulled apart by movement before any pressure exists; Brighton refused to offer that, because their shape stayed compact until the trigger moment.

In the “mid-block,” positioned +1 on the last line, but ready at any moment to transition into a high press upon a pressing trigger.

The steering began with Ayari. He curved his pressing run so that Konsa stayed in his cover shadow and Raya was forced to the other side. Kostoulas marked Gabriel, while Chema Andrés and Groß pushed aggressively onto Arsenal’s No. 8s. Groß in particular tracked the dropping Rice and at times advanced into the first pressing line, in some sequences all the way onto Konsa. That requires Rice to be picked up by a team-mate in the same moment – the man-marking worked through handovers as much as through tracking. Centrally, the striker and the No. 10 rotated accordingly: whoever had the shorter route to the next man on the ball pushed out, while the other covered behind him and took over again on the next trigger.

In a recent development, it only held up because the centre-backs came with it. Vušković and Struijk stepped out onto Ødegaard and the dropping Havertz and prevented an underload in central areas. When Arsenal built with three in the first line, Brighton kept one centre-back zonal in the back line – but with permanent reference to the unmarked player in the No. 6 space, stepping onto him the moment the press was triggered. Arsenal’s numerical advantage in build-up therefore never translated into a free man anywhere on the pitch.

Recent findings suggest that raya was part of the marking scheme too. Ayari’s cover shadow left only the route through a No. 6, and under man-marking that is not an escape but a duel that begins with the first touch. Raya’s body shape reinforced it: he tended to open only half-way, which effectively removed the switch to the far side from his repertoire. Steered onto his right foot, only the right-hand build-up side remained; the left lay open for long stretches and was unreachable for the one player who could have found it.

In a recent development, every back pass served as a trigger. When the ball went back to Raya or the centre-backs, Brighton pushed up as a unit and raised the defensive line. The density around the ball came less from the base shape than from the recovery runs: players who had been beaten sprinted back, and they did not run at the ball but with a cover shadow onto the lay-off option behind it. An Arsenal player with a marker in his back therefore had neither the lay-off nor the chance to turn.

Recent findings suggest that this is precisely where Brighton differed from most sides who get played through against Arsenal. The usual response is to stay deep once a line has been broken and wait for the shape to settle. Brighton instead pushed up into the next line and used the mid-block to prepare the next jump back into the high press – even when that press had just been beaten. The press therefore had not one starting point per possession, but a steady supply of new ones, and Arsenal had to solve the same pressure several times within a single attack.

According to recent reports, arsenal’s core problem was the absence of a threat in behind. Their attempts to play through the press came without pace beyond the back line, so Brighton were never forced to turn towards their own goal. That made the press cheap: no threat in behind, therefore no need to drop the line. There are three answers to committed man-marking – movement that drags your own marker away and opens space for a third player, a dribble that beats the assignment one-on-one, or a target man who wins the long balls. Arsenal produced none of them.

When the high press was beaten, Brighton dropped into a 5-1-4 and inverted the priority. The five in the last line formed a deliberate overload against Arsenal’s front line – in exactly the moment a man-oriented side is most vulnerable, because its players are facing forward while the opponents are already moving. Brighton took the depth out of the situation first and only then thought about the ball again.

In a recent development, A “mid-block” in a 5-1-4 formation. The foremost players protected the “red zone” by using their cover shadows and shifting extremely compactly. Arsenal was mostly forced to play around the block, repeatedly giving Brighton time to reorganize.

A single No. 6 held the connection in front, while the four most advanced players stayed narrow and closed the centre with cover shadows rather than pressing the ball carrier. Arsenal found no central switch on the ball-near side and had to play around the block. Every trip around it cost seconds that Brighton used to shift across, so the end of the route offered the same congestion as the start. In some phases six players stood in the last line.

Sources indicate that the block was not a terminus. At every Arsenal back pass Brighton jumped out again and restarted the high press – the same trigger as in the high phase, only from a deeper starting position. The spare man in the last line made that possible, usually Vušković: because the overload left him without a fixed opponent, he could step out, cover the depth and pick up a man himself a moment later. That freed a midfielder to push forward without leaving an assignment open behind him – precisely the point at which sides with a similar approach usually come apart.

According to recent reports, in the “mid-block” phase, the “+1” players organized themselves to execute early handovers and jump into pressing situations. Here, Vuskovic—acting as the “+1” player from the defensive line—steps up to pick up the Arsenal player operating in the number 10 position.

Recent findings suggest that on top of that came the trap on the touchline. Once Brighton steered the ball wide, players jumped in from every direction: the ball-near winger closed the route back, the No. 6 covered inside, the back line stepped out. The back pass, the switch and the ball in behind did not disappear one after another but at the same time. Take away only the back pass and a side switches play; take away only the switch and they play backwards and start again. When all that remains is an individual action against several opponents with the touchline at your back, it almost always ends with the opposition.

Recent findings suggest that after a regain there are two basic options: risk the ball immediately to launch the attack, or secure it to establish order. Hürzeler consistently chose the first, and it follows directly from the overall idea – a secured ball would have given Arsenal exactly the seconds in which their structure reorganises.

When a high press was bypassed, Brighton succeeded in forcing Arsenal into congested situations in the area in front of the back four. In doing so, the players who had been bypassed shifted to block the passing lanes of the players positioned behind the ball. This created additional pressure on the ball carrier, who was simultaneously facing pressure from the front via a “negative” pressing movement (i.e., pressing towards their own goal).

Sources indicate that the counter was prepared before the regain. When Arsenal found a player in the No. 6 space after beating the press, Brighton immediately closed his back pass, so the turnover inevitably occurred in a moment when Arsenal were all ahead of the ball. The density around the ball, a defensive necessity, meant in attack that Brighton were central and therefore on the shortest route to goal. The first ball went to the deepest player, followed by a dribble at speed into the box, with no intermediate step and no square pass for safety.

It has been revealed that in the build-up phase, Brighton utilized a diamond shape. De Cuyper and Boscagli engaged in a 2v2 duel on the left flank, while Kostoulas, Gomez, and Kadioglu created a high 3v3 situation on the right. Briefly, both center-backs and a defensive midfielder would spread out to widen the formation. Additional support occasionally came from Groß, dropping back from the number 10 position. Ayari occupied Konsa and Gabriel through constant runs into the open spaces ahead of him.

According to recent reports, in deep build-up Brighton baited Arsenal in deliberately. Verbruggen put his foot on the ball while the centre-backs split and lengthened the pressing runs of their opponents. On paper that produced a 3v2 against Arsenal’s first line – except Hürzeler had no intention of playing through that overload on the ground. 25 of 40 goalkeeper passes were long, 62.5 per cent, and they went overwhelmingly to the right.

The structure allowed for a long ball to the right flank, feeding into the 3-3 formation. This created opportunities to contest the second ball or flick on the aerial pass. Additionally, Vuskovic offered a short, low passing option as the free player.

Industry observers note that there, Brighton consistently created a 3v3 – an intact structure for the second ball regardless of whether the first contact was won. That is exactly what separates it from an ordinary long ball: the action was not judged by the aerial duel but by the situation that followed it. Kostoulas dropping added to the disorganisation of Arsenal’s high line, because a centre-back had to decide whether to follow him between the lines or let him turn. After winning second balls Brighton played on at high speed and looked for an early shot or an early cross, even against a defensive overload – again the decision for tempo over the clean attack.

It has been revealed that once again, the 3-3 structure on the right flank. Here, from open play.

According to recent reports, on the left Brighton worked through pinning rather than through length. Boscagli stepping inside dragged Saka into central areas and took him out of the wide zone Arsenal needed him in defensively, while De Cuyper dropped and offered the mid-range diagonal once the assignments had been pulled apart. The asymmetry was a personnel decision: the players for second balls were on the right, the players who could drag markers out of position on the left. Arsenal would have had to condense against one side and hand over assignments cleanly against the other.

The team’s build-up play was asymmetrical, featuring a high, wide approach on the right contrasted with the left flank: Boscagli often played an inverted role—supplementing the existing diamond formation—which opened up space for de Cuyper. Meanwhile, Groß and Kostoulas occupied the players on Arsenal’s right defensive flank, enabling Brighton to find low-ball solutions against the press.

In a recent development, with the ball in midfield there were two patterns. The first was the deliberate back pass to Verbruggen to pull Arsenal’s block out, followed by the same long-short structure as in deep build-up. The back pass was not a safety option here but the tool that created the space behind the pressing line in the first place.

The second pattern worked through central and wide tension at high speed, supplemented by rotations within their own structure. Arsenal repeatedly failed to hand over their pressing assignments in a coordinated way against it – the same weakness Brighton had solved cleanly in their own press. In possession Brighton’s shape approached a 4-3-3: Chema Andrés as the deepest No. 6, Groß with freedom from the left half-space, Kadıoğlu pushing up early to support Gómez, Boscagli starting slightly deeper on the left.

In a recent development, the 1-0 by Groß in the 31st minute is the whole blueprint in one sequence. Brighton play back to the goalkeeper from midfield, go long, lose the first contact and win the second ball. After a phase of circulation the next attack meets a back line that has already been destabilised: Kostoulas drops, Arsenal’s midfield and Konsa step out, and Kostoulas lays the ball back against the direction of the pressure to Groß. Because Ayari runs in behind at the same time, Arsenal’s defenders drop – and Groß has the time for the shot from around 20 metres. In the build-up Brighton had used rotations to drag Guimarães over to the left.

The opening goal stems from a positional attack. Kostoulas spots open space and makes a run into it. With a pass played across his standing leg, he feeds the ball to Groß in the space between the lines. As Groß takes a few quick touches and dribbles toward the defensive line, Gabriel and Calafiori drop back together, thereby opening up a shooting lane.

The 2-0 by Kostoulas shortly before half-time follows the same logic from the opposite direction. After a set piece of their own, Brighton clear an Arsenal counter and transition again immediately, 4v5 in Arsenal’s half, and once more the shot comes from distance while the centre-backs drop off.

Much like the goal that made it 1–0, both defenders went to ground near the ball carrier, thereby opening up space for the goalscorer—this time arising from a transition situation.

Sources indicate that both goals share the same cause: Arsenal’s centre-backs stepped out too late to press the man between the lines. React only when the shooting motion starts and you cannot get into the block from 20 to 25 metres. What is striking is that this passivity is the same one Arsenal revealed in their own build-up – a side that does not leave its position to offer itself does not leave it to close down a shooter either.

The 3-0 by Chema Andrés came from a corner: Groß delivered from the left, Brighton had created an overload at the far post and protected it with two blocks, and Chema rose completely unmarked to head in off the inside of the post.

Two goals up, many sides would have defended deeper. Brighton came out with unchanged and at times higher pressing intensity, and the coordination was visibly drilled: marking assignments were swapped cleanly even in dynamic situations, and Arsenal’s structural adjustments were absorbed.

It has been revealed that arsenal had managed a few organised possession phases in Brighton’s half in the first period; in the second it became harder. In those phases they built with a back three, Rice as the third centre-back, Ødegaard dropping alongside Guimarães and the full-backs occupying the half-spaces. Arteta reacted around the hour: Zubimendi and Merino for Timber and Guimarães, with Rice moving to right-back, followed shortly by Gyökeres and Eze for Ødegaard and Tzolis. There was no noticeable effect, because the problem did not lie in the shape but in the assignments in front of it.

There was also a layer that usually goes missing in analysis: Brighton used tactical fouls deliberately to stop Arsenal finding a rhythm. Arteta admitted afterwards that the game had been “very difficult to control”, pointing to lost first and second balls and to Brighton’s directness.

Arteta’s Arsenal being outplayed this clearly is rare. That it happened proactively and aggressively is rarer still – most sides who take something from Arsenal do it with a low block and efficiency. Hürzeler deliberately stepped back afterwards and praised his players’ courage, which gets to the heart of it: the blueprint only works if eleven players are willing to carry it through in every single sequence.

The interesting question is where the idea came from. Chelsea were a common opponent: Brighton had 74 per cent possession there and lost 3-4 against a counter-attacking side – control right down to the numbers, without return. Alonso’s Chelsea tried the opposite route against Arsenal, a deliberate surrender of control, also without success. The likely derivation lies between the two: neither give up control nor chase it, but generate the unsettled game state yourself and be prepared for it.

Sources indicate that there is no reason for panic at Arsenal, but Arteta will need answers against a high press. The build-up was predictable for long stretches, and above all the direct option with pace in behind was missing as a threat. As long as that does not exist, a man-oriented press costs very little against this side.

For Brighton the open question is repeatability. Man-marking of this commitment, collective recovery runs with cover shadows and a touchline trap that requires everyone to trigger at once are hard to produce twice in an English week. Whether the plan works was answered on this afternoon. How often it can be produced will decide the season.

Pot three teams will then find out their pot three and four opponents, before the pot four sides are allocated their fixtures against each other.

There are five English teams involved in the Champions League this season – one short of the Premier League’s tally from last term.

This season is the third under the newly introduced format, with a league phase instead of a group stage, and Uefa has confirmed that fixtures that have taken place in the league phase of the two previous seasons cannot be repeated this time around.

Liverpool, meanwhile, topped the league phase in the 2024-25 campaign – the first season with the fresh format – but fell at the first hurdle in the knockout stages after being drawn against Paris St-Germain.

The Ligue 1 side have proven that it’s not essential to be firing the whole way through the tournament, finishing 15th and 11th in the league phase in the last two seasons but going on to lift the trophy on both occasions.

Aspect analysis: Leipzig never found a trigger – LC

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart.
  • This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 20.10.2026 in den Kategorien Uncategorized mit 0 Kommentaren.

A 6-1 reads like a game in which everything fell apart. Look at how the goals came about one by one and a different picture emerges: it was not six separate problems but two or three, which Bayern punished in seven variations. No pressure on the man in possession, marking problems in central areas, and a back line that did not work with the movements in front of it – that chain runs through practically every goal conceded.

This aspect analysis therefore takes the goals rather than the game as its material and works back from there to the patterns.

In a recent development, bayern triggered very high throughout, stayed tight to their opponents and pushed through centrally without hesitation. Vandevoordt was pressed from Bayern’s right, with the clear intention of keeping him away from the left-hand build-up route and forcing the long ball. Leipzig’s front line of Nusa and Brajan Gruda repeatedly angled their runs deep against Nathaniel Brown and Konrad Laimer.

It has been revealed that bayern had one extra central player dropping into midfield in this phase, usually Kimmich. Had Leipzig played short to the right, he could have pressed through onto Raum; in practice he stayed central and pushed through from there. That left Leipzig with the long ball, and it was ineffective: it produced almost no regains, so the enforced forward play brought neither relief nor territory.

Going the other way, Leipzig got no access at all, and the reason was Bayern’s rotations. Kimmich dropped right, Pavlović left into a back three, with Upamecano holding a very wide position. Against this shifting three-man build-up Leipzig never found a trigger, because the assignments reset with every rotation – whoever was supposed to step out of midfield first had to work out who he was picking up. The handover of pressing duties out of central areas failed repeatedly.

In front of that, Bayern staggered their shape so that Leipzig’s compactness became the problem. Olise moved into the ten space at times, Nathaniel Brown operated in the half-lane and ran beyond from there, Luis Díaz stayed wide left. Saibari and Kane pinned several opponents centrally while regularly pulling out of the central lane. Because Leipzig pressed very narrow, this produced exactly what Bayern were looking for: once the opponent was committed near the ball, the switch followed, and on the now open side stood a one-on-one.

That already builds the bridge to the goals. The isolated one-on-ones in which Luis Díaz got his three finishes were not individual moments but the product of this sequence of pinning and switching.

It has been revealed that 1-0, Luis Díaz (12.) – The first goal already contains the full diagnosis. Kimmich receives centrally without any pressure and can turn out with an open body shape. Ahead of him Saibari and Kane occupy the central zone in front of the box, which forces Orban and Lukeba to step out – so far, the intended part. The full-backs, however, do not push up with that movement and stay too deep, while Raum’s position plays the runner onside. Klostermann stays outside and leaves the inside lane unsecured, and that is exactly where Luis Díaz starts from. Out of that unprotected lane Díaz runs into the back line and Kimmich chips the ball in behind. Not one bad decision, but four players whose decisions did not fit together.

2-0, Aleksandar Pavlović (26.) – Same cause, different route. Kane drops deep and Leipzig do not shift across as a unit – the reactions indicated it clearly: arms thrown up, gesturing, hands dropping again, the beginnings of frustration. Kane gets the free body shape, and with him the consequence is predictable: the long ball, high or flat. Because Leipzig are so narrow centrally, the ball flies straight through the entire zone in front of their back line. Luis Díaz moves actively into the passing lane to control it while Klostermann tries to get into his running line and does not make it – Díaz reaches the ball first. From the one-on-one he wins, Díaz dribbles centrally at Orban, which creates a four-against-three on the break. Díaz pins Orban and Lukeba centrally, Pavlović overlaps on the left after holding a high, left-leaning position all evening and threatening the back line. Two touches, left foot, finished away from the defender.

It has been revealed that 3-0, Michael Olise (34.) – Here Bayern’s press highlights itself at its clearest. From a Leipzig throw-in, the man-orientation is fully visible: consistent pushing through, clean handovers. A misplaced pass from Raum then cannot be defended, because neither the tracking nor the duelling is good enough to disturb the pass. Kane can open up half-way. Centrally, Olise comes inside from the wing, and Banzuzi and his partner fail to pick him up, letting him run through – against a player of that variability, an invitation to the key pass. Luis Díaz runs beyond and drags Orban with him, Klostermann is pinned wide by Saibari and can no longer get back into central areas. Olise finishes against the goalkeeper’s movement, across his standing leg into the far corner, catching Vandevoordt completely on the wrong foot.

4-0, Luis Díaz (47.) – After a regain, Bayern switch promptly to the far side and once diagonally through, putting Díaz in a one-on-one again. He holds the ball in the dribble, and Leipzig fail to solve the situation in three steps: the centre is not closed, Orban is too late stepping out, Klostermann does not get into the duel. That Vandevoordt leaves the far corner open is the final piece of an isolated one-on-one that should never have arisen.

Recent findings suggest that 5-0, Harry Kane (53.) – Structurally the most interesting goal. Leipzig play a long ball without preparing it and react to the consequences contradictorily: the back line does not push up at all, while the midfield line and both forwards counterpress forwards. The ten space opens up enormously, the gaps between the lines become huge – and Olise is standing in that zone. One pass from Kim is enough to take six Leipzig players out of the game. Olise runs unopposed at the back line and lays it off to Díaz, who is in a one-on-one again; Brown joins for the two-against-one and shifts into the inside lane. Klostermann does not pick up his run from the deep half-space, and centrally Kane again drops into Orban’s blind side – a pattern that stood out across the whole game. The result is a two-against-one against the goalkeeper.

It has been revealed that 6-0, Luis Díaz (69.) – From a set piece Bayern create a five-against-four out wide. Gnabry pins opponents and makes the space for Díaz, Orban again takes one substantial step in the block and does not get into the duel. The same scene as the 4-0, only from a different phase of play – a sign that this is a behavioural pattern rather than a snapshot.

6-1, Andrija Maksimović (90.+1) – Leipzig’s goal reveals in reverse what their own game had been missing. Bayern drop into a deeper block here, and Leipzig combine centrally before going wide. Gruda gets into a one-on-one against Brown, Upamecano steps across – but from above, with too wide a gap and without closing the centre. That opens the one-two, which Leipzig take immediately. Because the whole situation narrows onto that combination, the space behind it stays unoccupied, and Maksimović can take two touches on his left and finish unopposed.

It has been revealed that the sequence of goals reads like a repetition. Five of Bayern’s six come from the same combination of no pressure on the ball centrally and a back line that does not manage the space behind it. Luis Díaz stands in an isolated one-on-one three times, Orban is twice too late with a step that is too significant, Kane repeatedly drops into his blind side. Klostermann certainly did not have his best day – but it would be too easy to settle the bill with him. In the decisive scenes he faced situations that functioning protection in front of him should never have allowed to arise in the first place.

Behind it all lies not an individual problem but a structural one: Leipzig pressed narrow and found no trigger against Bayern’s rotating back three. That very compactness made the switch of play the opponent’s most effective tool, and at the end of every switch stood a one-on-one that Leipzig lost. The scoreline is not the story – the story is that the same scene worked six times.
